Statistical significance or effect size measures are appropriate proxies for clinical importance in sleep quality outcomes

questions.text: The populations in the studies cited (refs 1, 2, 3, 4) are representative of adults with chronic insomnia.
The melatonin formulations and doses used in the studies (refs 1, 2, 3, 4) are comparable to those used by the general adult population (e.g., immediate-release, over-the-counter).
The outcome measures of sleep quality in the studies (refs 1, 2, 3, 4) align with clinically meaningful improvements in overall sleep quality.
The positive results in populations with diverse medical conditions (ref 4) do not generalize to adults with chronic insomnia alone.
The results from studies on older adults (refs 5, 6) do not generalize to the general adult population with chronic insomnia.
The inclusion of ramelteon in some studies (ref 5) does not confound the assessment of melatonin's effects.
The clinical guidelines cited (refs 7, 8) are based on current and comprehensive evidence evaluations relevant to adults with chronic insomnia.
Improvements in sleep measures such as sleep-onset latency or total sleep time are not sufficient to constitute clinically important improvement in overall sleep quality.
Guidelines recommending against melatonin use are based on the same evidence base and interpret it consistently.
